title: A note on scenario convergence
text:
Exploring how GCAM scenarios diverge under different policy assumptions.

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# placeholder data — replace with actual GCAM output
scenarios <- expand.grid(
  year = 2020:2050,
  scenario = c("Reference", "NDC", "Net-zero 2060")
) |>
  mutate(emissions = case_when(
    scenario == "Reference" ~ 10 + 0.1 * (year - 2020),
    scenario == "NDC"       ~ 10 - 0.05 * (year - 2020),
    scenario == "Net-zero 2060" ~ 10 - 0.25 * (year - 2020)
  ))

ggplot(scenarios, aes(year, emissions, color = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "GtCO₂/yr", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

title: About
text:
I’ve spent the last decade working on energy transition in two of the most consequential places for global decarbonization: India and Saudi Arabia. The questions that occupy me sit between three domains that don’t always talk to each other — quantitative modeling of energy systems, applied policy analysis, and the strategic calculus of how governments and industry actually make decisions about emerging technologies.
My current work at KAPSARC focuses on Saudi Arabia’s transition strategy, with particular attention to hydrogen and CCUS ecosystems, the market structures needed to move from announcements to bankable projects, and how petrostate economies navigate decarbonization without conceding on energy security or economic diversification. Earlier work at CEEW and Brookings India was grounded in the equally difficult problem of how a large, coal-dependent, electricity-constrained economy builds a transition that is technically credible, politically viable, and aligned with development priorities.
Methodologically, I work primarily with integrated assessment frameworks (GCAM and related tools), techno-economic assessment, and scenario analysis. I care about models that are transparent, reproducible, and honest about what they can and cannot tell us — which is often less than policy conversations assume.

title: Powering Saudi Arabia’s EV future: the multi-billion investment roadmap for charging and batteries
text:
Saudi Arabia is undergoing a transformative shift in its road transport sector, aligning with the ambitious goals of Vision 2030 on economic diversification, environmental sustainability, and quality of life. As the Kingdom commits to a low-emission future, the widespread adoption of electric mobility is emerging as a central pillar.
A recent discussion paper, Scaling Up BEV Charging and Battery Capacity in Saudi Arabia, provides the first integrated estimate of the capital required to build out the necessary infrastructure — specifically Direct Current Fast Charging (DCFC) networks and domestic battery manufacturing — through 2060. The findings underscore that realizing the Kingdom’s EV ambitions will require sustained and well-coordinated investments.

title: Powering Saudi Arabia’s EV future: the multi-billion investment roadmap for charging and batteries
text:
Two pathways to electrification
The study uses scenario-based modeling to project passenger Battery Electric Vehicle (BEV) uptake under two long-term adoption pathways: Ambition and Ambition_plus. These scenarios reflect different levels of policy intensity and incorporate factors such as climate-adjusted battery degradation and technology cost reductions derived from learning curves.

The Ambition_plus scenario represents a more stringent policy framework: accelerated adoption, removal of institutional barriers for light-duty vehicles by 2035, and an Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) scrappage policy starting in 2030.

title: Powering Saudi Arabia’s EV future: the multi-billion investment roadmap for charging and batteries
section: The charging challenge: building the DCFC backbone
text:
The charging challenge: building the DCFC backbone
A robust public charging infrastructure is essential to support the transition, mitigating risks such as range anxiety and congestion. This paper focuses on DCFC — high-throughput fast charging crucial for intercity corridors and logistics hubs requiring rapid turnaround.
In the Saudi context, persistent high temperatures reinforce this choice. Brief, high-power sessions limit heat exposure for batteries and users, making DCFC preferable to prolonged Level 1 or Level 2 charging.
Cumulative investment needs between 2026 and 2060 are substantial:

title: Powering Saudi Arabia’s EV future: the multi-billion investment roadmap for charging and batteries
section: The manufacturing opportunity: localizing battery production
text:
The manufacturing opportunity: localizing battery production
The transition generates substantial battery demand not just from new vehicle sales but also from replacement needs — vehicles typically outlive their batteries. Saudi Arabia currently lacks scaled manufacturing capacity to meet this demand, meaning the transition initially depends heavily on imports.
The Kingdom is actively building capacity, with initiatives such as the Lucid plant in King Abdullah Economic City (KAEC) and the domestic EV brand Ceer anchoring local production. Domestic battery manufacturing matters because cells and packs dominate EV costs: capturing this share of the value chain allows the Kingdom to retain more of the transition’s economic benefits, with potential spillovers to stationary storage exports.
To meet cumulative demand of up to 853 GWh by 2060 under Ambition_plus, the required capital expenditure for domestic lithium-ion battery manufacturing is significant. The study evaluated two localization pathways:

title: Powering Saudi Arabia’s EV future: the multi-billion investment roadmap for charging and batteries
section: A strategic investment in non-oil GDP
text:
A strategic investment in non-oil GDP
Achieving high BEV penetration requires phasing investments: accelerating in the 2030s, moderating in the 2040s, and shifting toward renewal after 2050 — to avoid overbuilding while consistently meeting demand.
Strategic investment in this comprehensive BEV ecosystem — vehicles, batteries, and a nationwide DCFC backbone — is not only an environmental measure. It directly supports Vision 2030’s objective of increasing the non-oil share of GDP by catalyzing new, technology-driven value chains.
Large-scale electrification of Saudi Arabia’s passenger transport sector is both economically viable and operationally feasible — provided that policymakers and investors commit to the quantitative roadmap the analysis lays out.

This post summarizes findings from ongoing work at KAPSARC. For the underlying methodology and full modeling assumptions, see the discussion paper.

title: Research
text: My research examines the strategic, technical, and market dimensions of energy transition in emerging and oil-producing economies. Three themes organize most of the work: (i) decarbonization pathways and scenario analysis, typically using integrated assessment models; (ii) the ecosystem conditions — policy, regulation, market design — needed for emerging clean energy technologies such as hydrogen and CCUS to move from strategy to deployment; and (iii) the political economy of transition in coal-dependent and hydrocarbon-exporting contexts.

title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia’s cooling-driven energy future
text: One of the less-discussed dimensions of Saudi Arabia’s energy transition is that it is simultaneously an adaptation problem. The country faces both a decarbonization trajectory and a temperature trajectory — and the two interact in ways that conventional long-term electricity planning hasn’t fully absorbed. A recent study, Cooling the Kingdom: Long-term impacts of climate change on electricity demand and household expenditure in Saudi Arabia, examines this interaction using the GCAM-KSA integrated assessment model, tracing how rising temperatures and socioeconomic growth will reshape the nation’s energy landscape and household budgets through the end of the century.

title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia’s cooling-driven energy future
text:
The rising demand for cooling
The most striking projections concern Cooling Degree Days (CDD) — a measure of how much cooling is needed to maintain indoor comfort. Under a high-emissions pathway (RCP 7.0, roughly consistent with continued fossil-fuel expansion and limited mitigation), annual CDD in Saudi Arabia are projected to rise by 40% to 80% by 2100. Heating Degree Days (HDD), conversely, fall toward zero, effectively eliminating the need for space heating across most of the country.
This shift establishes space cooling as the dominant energy service required for indoor comfort. National cooling demand is expected to increase by up to 80% by 2100 compared to current levels. The drivers change over time: population and income growth drive demand in the early century, but the direct impact of climate change becomes the primary driver after 2060, particularly in high-warming scenarios.



Metric
Projected change by 2100 (RCP 7.0)




Cooling Degree Days (annual)
+40% to +80%


Heating Degree Days (annual)
Toward zero


National cooling demand
Up to +80% vs. current

Up to +20%

title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia’s cooling-driven energy future
section: Impact on building electricity and households
text:
Impact on building electricity and households
The surge in cooling needs translates directly into higher electricity demand. The research suggests that building electricity consumption could increase by as much as 20% due to climate impacts alone — separate from and additional to growth driven by population, income, and electrification of other end uses. This divergence becomes particularly pronounced in the second half of the century as cooling seasons lengthen and intensify.
For the average household, this means a tangible impact on discretionary budgets. Projections show that annual electricity expenditures could rise by 8% to 33%, depending on the specific climate and growth trajectory.
A subtler finding is worth drawing out: under the low-emissions RCP 2.6 pathway — consistent with Saudi Arabia’s net-zero target by 2060 — higher household expenditures are primarily linked to improved living standards and greater service access, not to the cost of coping with heat. In other words, aggressive mitigation reshapes why households spend more on electricity, not just whether they do.

title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia’s cooling-driven energy future
text:
A call for integrated planning
The findings argue that standard long-term planning practices are inadequate for a climate-constrained future. The study advocates for:

Integrating climate signals directly into long-term electricity planning and peak-load management, rather than treating them as exogenous shocks.
Strengthening building efficiency standards and promoting adaptive technologies — passive design, district cooling, higher-efficiency HVAC — to reduce the energy burden before it reaches the grid.
Targeting policy reforms to ensure that the low-carbon transition remains socially inclusive and affordable, given that cooling access has distributional consequences.

Anticipating these cooling needs now — rather than retrofitting responses after they emerge — aligns with Vision 2030’s efficiency objectives and the Kingdom’s net-zero commitments.

title: Staying cool in a warming Kingdom: Saudi Arabia’s cooling-driven energy future
section: What this study covers, and what it doesn’t
text:
What this study covers, and what it doesn’t
A brief note on scope for readers familiar with integrated assessment modeling: the analysis captures aggregate building electricity demand under temperature change but does not resolve sub-daily peak dynamics, which are increasingly the binding constraint on Saudi grid planning. It also treats the building stock at a relatively aggregated level — disaggregating by building type, vintage, and retrofit potential would sharpen the efficiency policy signal. These are natural next steps for the modeling agenda, not limitations of the current contribution.

This post summarizes findings from ongoing work at KAPSARC. For the underlying methodology and full modeling assumptions, see the discussion paper.
